tldr: In vision-language model (VLM) reinforcement learning, the authors developed "Rollplex", a runtime that spatially colocates the prefix computation of subsequent phases with rollout decoding by tapping into unused GPU compute capacity. By optimizing memory management and weight sharing without breaking synchronous on-policy semantics, it achieves speedups of up to 1.30× over serial execution and up to 2.24× over disaggregated execution under the same GPU budget.
hero_caption: GPU memory consumption over time for Rollplex and four ablations. Naive concurrent execution (top four variants) exceeds the 80 GB HBM capacity and crashes with out-of-memory (OOM) errors. In contrast, Rollplex (middle and bottom) keeps memory within bounds and runs reliably through phase-aware lifecycle management.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for vision-language models (VLMs) handling video and images is drawing heavy interest for robotic visual action and embodied AI. Traditional RL frameworks built for LLMs execute the rollout (response generation), reference scoring, and actor training phases in strict serial order. While this works well for text-only RL where autoregressive response decoding dominates execution time, the equation flips completely for VLMs, where encoding dense video frames and processing long prompt prefixes make up 79% to 98% of the sequence.

A key insight here is that the prefix computation in reference scoring and training actor phases does not depend on the response tokens being generated by rollout. Furthermore, during rollout decoding, GPU streaming multiprocessor (SM) utilization drops below 20%, leaving plenty of compute headroom. Capitalizing on this, the authors designed Rollplex, a runtime that moves the prefix computation of subsequent phases forward to run alongside rollout decoding on the same GPUs. However, a naive concurrent launch inflates memory requirements to roughly 165 GiB per GPU—far exceeding the 80 GB HBM limit—and hits a wall because rollout and training prefer different tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and weight layouts.

Rollplex overcomes these hurdles with precise memory lifecycle management using CUDA VMM and a parallelism-aware weight-sharing mechanism that reconciles differences in TP degree. In experiments training Qwen2.5-VL-32B across 32 H800 GPUs, it achieved 1.23× to 1.30× step-time speedups over serial colocation and 1.57× to 2.24× over disaggregated execution, all while fully preserving the synchronous on-policy semantics and validation reward trajectory.
contributions: Formulated an execution model tailored to the input-heavy workload of VLM RL that overlaps prefix computation of subsequent phases with rollout decoding while preserving synchronous on-policy semantics.
Designed a phase-aware memory management mechanism that retains only necessary intermediate tensors in HBM, offloads unneeded state, and streams optimizer updates in chunks.

Developed a parallelism-aware weight sharing mechanism that allows rollout and training to use different tensor-parallel degrees (e.g., TP=4 vs. TP=8) while physically sharing the vast majority (about 93%) of actor weight memory.
Demonstrated on 32 H800 GPUs that Rollplex delivers speedups of up to 1.30× over serial colocation and up to 2.24× over disaggregation on real workloads while maintaining exact on-policy updates.

sections.heading: Why is conventional RL execution inefficient for VLMs?
sections.summary: Because VLM reinforcement learning is dominated by processing dense video inputs and prompt prefixes, conventional phase-granular serial execution wastes substantial GPU compute capacity. Overlapping prefix computation—which does not depend on the generated response—with rollout decoding enables significant speedups while preserving synchronous execution.
sections.details:
Research using VLMs as robotic action policies is advancing rapidly, as seen in models like PaLM-E, RT-2, and OpenVLA. Post-training with reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial to boosting their capabilities, yet existing distributed RL frameworks (such as DeepSpeed-Chat, verl, and ROLL) were designed around text LLMs and run rollout, reference scoring, and training in strict serial phases.

While output token generation (decoding) takes up most of the time in text RL, video VLMs fundamentally change the workload profile. In four video tasks investigated in this paper, prompt tokens accounted for 79% to 98% of the entire sequence. In other words, input prefix processing is extremely heavy. Crucially, the prefix computation performed by the reference model and the training actor has zero dependency on the response tokens generated by rollout. It can therefore be computed ahead of time without waiting for rollout decoding to finish.

However, naively attempting to run these workloads simultaneously runs into three major obstacles:
- The memory capacity wall: colocating all phase tensors simultaneously consumes roughly 165 GiB per GPU, easily blowing past the 80 GB limit of an H800.
- Tensor parallelism (TP) mismatch: rollout prefers a smaller TP degree (TP=4) to minimize communication overhead, whereas training prefers a larger TP degree (TP=8) to distribute memory footprint.
- Resource contention: if prefix processing slows down decoding too much, the overall critical path is extended.

Rollplex overcomes these challenges through fine-grained memory management and an intelligent weight-sharing mechanism.

sections.heading: The decoding opportunity and the hurdles in the way
sections.summary: While prompt computation dominates video VLM reinforcement learning, GPU compute (SM) utilization during rollout decoding drops below 20%. This compute headroom offers an ideal window to overlap prefix processing, but doing so faces severe memory pressure reaching 165 GiB and tensor parallelism mismatches.
sections.details:
One iteration of synchronous on-policy RL (such as GRPO) follows a strict sequence: rollout using the latest model $\theta_k$, KL regularization scoring via a reference model, loss computation, backpropagation, and an optimizer update. In VLMs, a vision encoder (ViT) sits in front of the language model, converting a 16-frame block of 720p video into approximately 1,536 vision tokens.

Empirical profiles show that in text tasks like GSM8K, the median prompt length is only 60 to 90 tokens (11% to 19% of the sequence). In video tasks, however, it reaches 470 to 5,900 tokens (79% to 98% of the sequence). Input processing is overwhelmingly heavy.

At the same time, profiling the sequential rollout decode phase reveals that generating tokens one by one is memory-bandwidth bound, with Tensor Core and active SM utilization remaining below 19% (Figure F3). In contrast, video encoding and prompt prefill are compute-dense matrix multiplications. The resource demands of the two workloads complement each other neatly.

However, a naive colocation of Qwen2.5-VL-32B requires about 165 GiB of HBM to hold the rollout KV cache, prefix boundary KV, intermediate activations for backpropagation, model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states all at once (Table 1). On top of that, training wants TP=8 while rollout wants TP=4, raising the challenge of how to share weights without maintaining duplicate copies in memory.

captions.F3: Timeline of GPU resource utilization during rollout decoding. While memory bandwidth (BW) sees moderate use, Tensor Core (TC) and active SM (Act SM%) utilization remain extremely low (below 20%), revealing significant idle compute capacity.

sections.heading: Cross-phase execution scheduling and two core technologies
sections.summary: Rollplex executes prefix computation of subsequent phases during rollout, retaining only boundary states to stitch into later suffix processing. This design is enabled by two mechanisms: phase-aware memory management and parallelism-aware weight sharing.
sections.details:
Rollplex orchestrates inter-process execution across a single pool of GPUs within the same node.

### 3.1. Cross-Phase Execution Scheduling
The workflow is restructured into three phases:
- Phase 1: While rollout decodes the response, the reference model and training actor run video encoding and prompt prefill (prefix computation) concurrently. The generated boundary KV cache and log probabilities are retained. For the training actor, the autograd backward graph is kept intact, but bulky activation tensors are offloaded to host memory.
- Phase 2: Once rollout finishes, reference scoring and training forward/backward passes run only on the generated response (suffix). Rollout KV caches and related buffers are freed immediately at this point.
- Phase 3: Optimizer updates are executed in a pipelined, chunked streaming fashion to produce a new BF16 weight snapshot $\theta_{k+1}$.

### 3.2. Phase-Aware Memory Management
Tensor residency in HBM is restricted strictly to its interval from first critical use to last consumption. Using CUDA VMM (Virtual Memory Management), physical HBM pages are dynamically allocated and mapped without altering virtual address pointers.
During the optimizer step—the point of peak memory pressure—Rollplex avoids loading FP32 master weights and Adam moments all at once. Instead, it partitions parameters into equal-sized chunks. Pipelining computation on chunk $j$ with data transfers for chunk $j+1$ dramatically slashes the optimizer's memory footprint.

### 3.3. Parallelism-Aware Weight Sharing
To physically share weight storage between training (TP=8) and rollout (TP=4), tensor layouts are categorized into three cases and mapped via CUDA IPC:
- Case 1 (Identical / Nested Sharding): When both share identical split axes, such as in the vision encoder, they share the exact same physical memory.
- Case 2 (Transposed Layout): For row-parallel weights, storing the weight layout in transposed form allows it to appear contiguous to both processes, enabling zero-copy sharing via GEMM transpose flags.
- Case 3 (Incompatible Permutations): Only tensors whose physical layouts do not align—such as interleaved QKV attention heads (representing 7.2% of weights)—are copied and permuted into a rollout buffer after updates.
This setup enables execution across differing TP degrees with almost zero weight duplication.

sections.heading: Real-world hardware results on speedups and memory reduction
sections.summary: Experiments on 32 H800 GPUs with Qwen2.5-VL-32B demonstrated 1.23× to 1.30× step-time reductions over serial colocation and 1.57× to 2.24× over disaggregation. Training convergence and reward curves matched baseline runs exactly.
sections.details:
The evaluation ran on 32 NVIDIA H800 GPUs (4 nodes) using Qwen2.5-VL-32B and the GRPO algorithm (8 responses per prompt). Four benchmark datasets were used: CLEVRER, PerceptionTest, LLaVA-Video-178K, and STAR.

### 4.2. End-to-End Performance
Under the same 32-GPU budget, Rollplex achieved 1.23× to 1.30× speedups over conventional serial colocation (Colocate) and 1.57× to 2.24× over disaggregated setups (Disagg) where nodes are split between rollout and training pools. In Disagg, efficiency drops heavily because one pool sits completely idle while the other is active.

### 4.3. Impact on Training Quality
Because Rollplex changes only the execution schedule without altering computational logic, the algorithm's strict on-policy semantics are fully preserved. Across all four datasets, step-by-step validation reward differences remained near zero, and learning trajectories tracked the baseline perfectly.

### 4.4. Memory Feasibility (Ablations)
As shown in Figure F8, turning off any single mechanism—"No Offload", "Resident vLLM", "Unchunked Optimizer", or "No Weight Sharing"—breaches the 80 GB ceiling and triggers an OOM failure. Only with all Rollplex mechanisms active does the workload complete safely under 80 GB. Under weight sharing, 92.8% of all parameters were shared with zero copies under Cases 1 and 2.

### 4.5. Analysis of Parallelism and Resource Sharing Policies
Running rollout at TP=8 slows decoding down by 1.17× to 1.31× due to communication overhead. Rollplex allows rollout to stay at TP=4, yielding up to a 1.17× reduction in overall step time. Furthermore, static MPS partitioning (capping SM allocation) caused steep performance penalties; unconstrained MPS-Default proved most effective at harvesting idle compute capacity dynamically.

captions.F8: GPU memory usage over time across different methods. Four ablation baselines with mechanisms disabled (top) exceed the 80 GB HBM limit (dashed line) during optimizer execution and crash, whereas Rollplex (middle) stays strictly within bounds. The bottom graph breaks down memory usage by role.

sections.heading: Applicability conditions, robotics implications, and limitations
sections.summary: Rollplex delivers its greatest gains on workloads with heavy prompt and video inputs, fitting well with long-trajectory robotic decision-making (VLA). At the same time, sharing a single GPU across processes introduces challenges around fault isolation.
sections.details:
Rollplex is most effective when two conditions hold: a large fraction of training computation is spent on prefix processing that does not depend on the generated response, and the GPU budget is constrained such that separate dedicated node pools cannot be maintained for rollout and training. The benefits diminish for short-prompt text tasks or in settings with abundant GPU capacity.

In robotics, vision-language-action (VLA) models undergoing RL over extended trajectories represent a prime target. Context like past visual observations, instructions, and history is fixed and independent of the current response, allowing Rollplex to reclaim idle compute during action decoding. However, in closed-loop setups where future observations depend on earlier actions, trajectory-aware KV cache management would be required.

A current limitation is fault propagation (blast radius). Because Rollplex logically shares the same GPU across processes using CUDA IPC and MPS, a fatal CUDA exception or communication deadlock in any single process can take down the entire node and fail the iteration. Isolating process failures and building recovery mechanisms remain important future work.

sections.heading: Positioning among RL runtimes and GPU spatial sharing research
sections.summary: Unlike earlier LLM RL frameworks that rely on phase-granular serial execution or asynchronous policy updates, this work decomposes intra-iteration dependencies to spatially overlap them. It also differs distinctly from serving-oriented prefill/decode disaggregation.
sections.details:
Distributed RL frameworks have historically relied on temporal sharing (e.g., verl, ROLL), physical node disaggregation (e.g., OpenRLHF), or asynchronous updates that relax ordering constraints to boost throughput. However, these systems either preserve phase-by-phase serial execution or compromise on-policy semantics by updating on stale policies. Rollplex stands apart by overlapping intra-iteration phases spatially while maintaining 100% synchronous on-policy fidelity.

For GPU spatial sharing, technologies like NVIDIA MPS and MIG are designed to run independent jobs fairly; they are not tailored for cooperating processes with interdependencies and autograd backward graphs. Moreover, while prefill/decode disaggregation in LLM inference (e.g., chunked prefill) focuses on load-smoothing across distinct requests, Rollplex's uniqueness lies in shifting resources across different roles within the exact same reinforcement learning context.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new standard runtime for VLM reinforcement learning
sections.summary: The authors introduced Rollplex, a runtime that overlaps prefix computation with rollout decoding in VLM reinforcement learning. Delivering up to 1.30× speedup over serial colocation and up to 2.24× over disaggregation on 32 H800 GPUs, it establishes a high-performance foundation for synchronous RL.
sections.details:
This paper highlighted the "input-heavy" profile unique to VLM reinforcement learning with dense video inputs, and introduced Rollplex to harvest idle compute capacity during rollout decoding by running subsequent prefix computation ahead of time.

Phase-aware memory management circumvents HBM capacity ceilings, while parallelism-aware weight sharing reconciles the conflicting parallelism preferences of rollout (TP=4) and training (TP=8). Experiments on 32 H800 GPUs training Qwen2.5-VL-32B proved that Rollplex achieves 1.23× to 1.30× speedups over serial colocation and 1.57× to 2.24× over node-disaggregated configurations without compromising on-policy update correctness. It provides a vital systems foundation for scaling embodied AI and robot learning.

sections.heading: Appendix: Complete tensor lifecycle design
sections.summary: The appendix outlines a comprehensive tensor lifecycle contract (Table 3), specifying when each tensor is allocated, consumed, attached to the autograd graph, and mapped. This rigorous schedule explains how concurrent execution in Phase 1 avoids out-of-memory errors.
sections.details:
The appendix details the precise tensor lifecycle contract enforced by Rollplex across Phases 1 through 3:

- Inference-only states (rollout KV cache): Resident in HBM only during generation, requiring no autograd tracking, and discarded immediately once generation concludes.
- Boundary states (prefix boundary KV, log probabilities): Computed in Phase 1 and retained in HBM until consumed during Phase 2 suffix processing. Only the training actor's KV tensors remain attached to the autograd graph for backward gradient propagation.
- Large training states (activations, gradients, FP32 optimizer states): Offloaded to host memory immediately upon creation or discarded for checkpoint recomputation. Optimizer states are streamed into HBM strictly in chunks during Phase 3.
- Regenerable states (BF16 model weights, reference model weights): Reference weights are paged in only during their active window. Stale BF16 actor weights are discarded upon entering Phase 3, allowing their buffer to be repurposed for optimizer operations.

This disciplined lifecycle ensures that even during Phase 1 peak concurrency, HBM holds only the rollout KV, boundary KV, shared actor weights, and transient reference weights, preventing memory exhaustion.

takeaways: In video VLM and robot reinforcement learning, input processing (prompts and observations) consumes over 80% of the sequence, making prefix hiding just as vital as decode acceleration.

Because GPU streaming multiprocessors (SMs) sit largely idle during rollout decoding, running independent subsequent prefix computations during this window provides "free" forward progress without breaking synchronous semantics.

Tensor parallelism mismatches between rollout (preferring smaller TP) and training (preferring larger TP) can be bridged without duplicating model weights by using transposed memory views and CUDA VMM.
When spatially sharing a GPU across concurrent tasks, imposing static SM limits degrades throughput; unconstrained MPS (Default) handles dynamic opportunistic compute harvesting far more effectively.
limitations: The performance gains diminish on text-only workloads with short prefixes dominated by decoding, or in setups with ample GPU pools where node disaggregation causes negligible idle waste.
Because processes share the physical GPU via CUDA IPC and MPS, an unrecoverable CUDA exception in one process brings down the entire node pool, posing a fault isolation challenge.
In closed-loop robot control environments where subsequent visual observations depend dynamically on previous actions, the KV cache management strategy will require further extension.
